column1: # The Node differential oracle's dispositions: every expression the dialect
# rejects statically (`reject`) or at run time (`runtime-reject`), with the
# diagnostic it must name. Every other expression is `accept`. `generate.mjs`
# reads this file, and `differential_oracle.rs` holds the table to it, so a
# disposition cannot change in the table without changing here, where the
# regeneration reads it.
# expression (JSON)
'ab'.map((x) => x)
null ?? 1 || 2
/a/d
/a/v
new RegExp(/a/g)
# Splitting an astral character into units would manufacture a lone
# surrogate, which the UTF-8 value model cannot represent. This is the
# existing shape-dependent runtime rejection, not a withdrawn method.
'\\uD83D\\uDE00'.split('')
# Node's `JSON.parse` creates `__proto__` as an ordinary own data property.
# This value model has no prototype chain, so every read of that name already
# refused; the key is now refused where the value enters instead, so a parsed
# object can never hold a key that `Object.keys` lists and nothing can read
# back. A registered over-rejection, not a conformance claim.
JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{\__proto__\":1,\"a\":2}'))"
Object.keys(JSON.parse('{\a\":1,\"__proto__\":2}')).join(',')"
# FIG-3604: a closure copies what it captures, so one created before its
# binding is reassigned refuses rather than reading the stale copy (register
# entry 5, the read path).
(() => { let x = 1; const f = () => x; x = 2; return f(); })()
# The closed-shape field guard (FIG-3626, ADR 0062 register entry 22): a read
# or write of a field a statically closed object literal lacks is refused at
# link, as TypeScript's checker refuses it. These rows still run Node-exact
# through the VM (an open object reaches the same paths), and a cell refuses
# them at link by name. A literal that a spread, a computed key, a
# computed-key write or an escape opens reads as JavaScript does: those rows
# are ordinary `accept` rows.
({a:1}).missing
# FIG-3652: a function's string is its source text, which the runtime does
# not keep; converting one to a primitive refuses by name. A built-in method
# value is a function too, so the same ruling covers it (FIG-3701).
'' + function () { return 1; }
String([].map)
# FIG-3650/FIG-3651: ECMA-262 early errors reject as TS_SYNTAX_ERROR; the two
# forms tsc --strict rejects (TS2393/TS2300, TS2703) refuse by name.
(() => { switch (0) { case 1: let f; default: var f; } })()
(() => { try {} catch (e) { let e; } })()
(() => { for (let x of []) { var x; } })()
(() => { 'use strict'; return '\\8'; })()
(async () => { var \\u0061wait; })()
(() => { function f() { return 1; } function f() { return 2; } return f(); })()
(() => delete 1)()
# Invalid escapes are a SyntaxError in an untagged template (the raw form is
# reserved for tags, which are refused), and a cooked lone surrogate is as
# unrepresentable as the string-literal form (FIG-3720).
`\\unicode`
# FIG-3704: a GetSetRecord-valid set-like object still cannot be a Set
# argument — its `has`/`keys` are guest closures and a synchronous builtin
# cannot invoke them — so the method refuses by name rather than silently
# computing the wrong set.
(() => { const o={size:1,has:()=>true,keys:()=>[9]}; return [...new Set([1]).union(o)].join(','); })()
# FIG-3656: `new Number` is a boxed-primitive constructor the value model
# does not admit — the compiler refuses it outright — and a `{}` literal's
# `constructor` read is a static link refusal.
typeof new Number(1)
(() => { try { return new Number(1).toFixed(101); } catch (e) { return e instanceof RangeError; } })()
({}).constructor === Object
